title: Perfectionism in Moral and Political Philosophy

summaries.example: Imagine two school clubs. One club only asks, “What do students enjoy?” Another also asks whether activities help students learn, make things, understand ideas, and build good friendships. The second club is thinking in a perfectionist way: it sees some parts of a good life as valuable even when people do not already want them.
summaries.summary: Moral and political perfectionism says that some activities, relationships, achievements, or ways of living are valuable in themselves. They are not valuable only because someone desires them or feels pleasure from them. The entry explains two main ways to understand human perfection. One connects good lives with developing human nature, such as reasoning and other important capacities. The other identifies a group of objective goods, such as knowledge, friendship, art, or culture, without saying that all of them come from one account of human nature. Perfectionism does not require everyone to live in exactly the same way. Different people may flourish through different talents and goals, and some goods may be equally valuable or difficult to compare. The entry also asks whether moral rules should tell us to improve ourselves and help others, and whether governments should promote valuable ways of living. Supporters and critics debate fairness, freedom, respect, and the danger of government control.
key_ideas: Perfectionists think some things are good even when people do not desire them.
A good human life can mean more than feeling happy or getting what one wants.
People may become excellent in different ways, such as through art, study, athletics, friendship, or helping others.
Perfectionism can guide personal choices, moral duties, and government policies.
Philosophers disagree about whether governments should promote good ways of living.
summaries.why_it_matters: This idea matters because it asks what makes a life genuinely good. It reminds us to think about learning, friendship, creativity, character, and service—not only about pleasure or getting what we want. It also raises an important public question: when leaders believe some activities are valuable, should they encourage them, or should people be free to choose their own paths? The entry does not settle these disagreements, but it shows why they are difficult.

important_terms.definition: The view that some ways of living, activities, or relationships are good in themselves, not only because people want or enjoy them.
A life that develops abilities, takes part in worthwhile activities, and succeeds in valuable relationships or goals.
The idea that several different kinds of life can be good, even if no single kind is best for everyone.
The idea that a government should avoid choosing one disputed idea of a good life for everyone.

questions_to_think_about: Can something be good for a person even if that person does not want it?
Can two very different lives both be excellent?
Should a government support valuable activities, or should it stay neutral?
How can people be encouraged without being unfairly controlled?

summaries.example: Suppose a government considers funding public libraries, museums, and scientific research. A perfectionist may support this because knowledge, art, and cultural achievement are objective goods that help create excellent human lives, even if not every citizen prefers them. A critic may worry that public policy should remain neutral among reasonable conceptions of the good, especially when citizens disagree. A perfectionist could still accept pluralism and argue that government should support several valuable possibilities rather than impose one complete way of life.
summaries.summary: The entry presents perfectionism as a theory that some goods are objectively valuable: their value does not depend simply on being desired, enjoyed, or experienced as pleasant. In its humanistic form, perfectionism concerns the components of an excellent human life. One version grounds these goods in the development of human nature; another identifies objective goods without relying on such a theory. Both views face a central explanatory question: why do particular capacities, activities, or goods deserve this status? Perfectionism need not be monistic. Human nature may be expressed through different pursuits, and objective goods may be equal, incomparable, or combined in different proportions. Thus several forms of life can be excellent, although perfectionism still excludes some ways of living as not valuable merely because they are chosen. As an ethical theory, perfectionism can require self-development and concern for others. It may aim at maximizing human perfection, allow some priority to one’s own life, or combine perfectionist aims with constraints against harming or sacrificing people. As a political theory, it supports the possibility that institutions may promote objective goods. Its main rivals defend state neutrality, often because citizens reasonably disagree and because respecting persons may require political justification from common ground. The entry examines whether neutrality, liberty, autonomy, self-respect, ethical independence, or the limits of government provide decisive objections. It concludes that the connections among value theory, ethics, and politics are not automatic: one may accept one part of perfectionism while rejecting another.
key_ideas: Perfectionism is first a theory of value, but it can also become a moral theory or a theory of politics.
Human nature perfectionism and objective goods perfectionism offer different explanations of what makes a life excellent; each faces its own explanatory challenge.
Perfectionism is compatible with pluralism. Different people may develop different capacities, combine goods differently, or pursue goods that cannot be ranked precisely.

Perfectionist ethics may be egoistic, non-egoistic, consequentialist, deontological, or part of a mixed moral theory. These versions differ over how to balance self-development, concern for others, and respect for persons.

Perfectionist politics rejects a general ban on promoting the good, but it must answer objections about liberty, coercion, manipulation, self-respect, ethical independence, and governmental competence.

Perfectionism and equality are not automatically opposed. Some versions favor inequality, while others argue that equality helps everyone develop or that independent egalitarian principles should limit perfectionist policies.
summaries.why_it_matters: Perfectionism addresses a basic philosophical question: is a satisfying life simply one in which a person gets what they want, or are some ways of living better for reasons that do not depend on personal preference? Its political implications are equally important. If knowledge, art, friendship, autonomy, or other goods matter objectively, public institutions might have reasons to support them. Yet such support can threaten liberty, equal standing, or the ability to form one’s own life. Studying the debate clarifies why disagreements about education, culture, public funding, personal choice, and state power cannot be resolved by appealing to only one value.

important_terms.definition: A family of views claiming that some activities, relationships, achievements, or states of affairs are valuable in themselves, not merely because they are desired or pleasurable.
A view that identifies the good life with developing capacities or features understood as central to human nature, often including rational capacities.
A view that identifies a range of objectively valuable goods without explaining their value through a theory of human nature.
The position that there may be several valuable, equally good, or incomparable forms of human life rather than one uniquely best life.
A moral approach directing people to protect or promote objectively good human lives, including their own and, in some versions, the lives of others.
The claim that the state should not promote a disputed conception of the good, or should justify political action without relying on such a conception.
A moral limit on coercion often understood as allowing government interference only to prevent clear and direct harm to others.
A condition proposed by some critics: an activity contributes to a life only when the person endorses its value, or at least is not alienated from it.

questions_to_think_about: Does an objective account of human goods threaten individual freedom, or can it support meaningful freedom?
Can a society promote excellence while recognizing several reasonable forms of life?
Should the value of greater achievement receive greater moral weight, or should each person’s development count equally?
When does helping people choose well become manipulation or paternalism?
Could a government’s attempt to promote good lives be self-defeating if valuable activities require personal endorsement?

summaries.example: A town must decide how to spend money. One plan gives every teenager the same small entertainment voucher. Another funds a library, music lessons, sports spaces, and youth groups. A perfectionist might say the second plan is better because learning, creativity, health, and friendship are valuable parts of a good life, even when not everyone asks for them. A critic might reply that families and young people should choose their own activities, especially when reasonable people disagree about what is most valuable.
summaries.summary: Perfectionism in moral and political philosophy begins with a claim about value: some activities, relationships, achievements, and ways of living are good in themselves. They are not good just because people desire them, enjoy them, or experience pleasure from them. The source focuses especially on the good of human lives. It distinguishes a life that goes well for its owner from an excellent life, which can also involve worthwhile achievement, relationships, or sacrifice for other people and valuable goals. Two important versions are discussed. Human nature perfectionism connects valuable goods with the development of human capacities. Objective goods perfectionism identifies valuable things without making human nature the explanation. Both views must explain why their chosen goods count as objective goods. Perfectionism does not necessarily say that everyone should follow one identical life plan. Different people may develop different abilities, combine goods in different ways, or pursue goods that cannot be compared exactly. This supports value pluralism, though perfectionism still says that some ways of living are not valuable merely because someone chooses them. In ethics, perfectionism may direct people to improve themselves and sometimes to promote the good of others. In politics, it challenges the idea that the state must always remain neutral among competing ideas of a good life. Critics worry that such policies could interfere with freedom, disrespect citizens, or manipulate their choices. Perfectionists respond that government can sometimes support valuable options, protect the conditions for development, or promote autonomy itself. The source presents these arguments as continuing disputes rather than as questions with one settled answer.
key_ideas: Perfectionism contrasts with views that define the good only through pleasure or desire satisfaction.
The source distinguishes a good life measured by well-being from an excellent life that may include sacrifice for other people or valuable goals.
Perfectionists can disagree about which goods matter and how much they matter.
A perfectionist view can allow many different successful lifestyles rather than one model for everyone.
In politics, perfectionists permit government efforts to promote the good in principle, while critics emphasize neutrality, liberty, respect, and independence.
The debate is not simply perfectionism versus freedom: some perfectionists treat autonomy and self-direction as important parts of a good life.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate helps explain why people disagree about what society should value. Some think government should focus on fair rules while leaving each person to choose a life plan. Others think public institutions may rightly support education, art, science, friendship, health, or other valuable parts of human life. Perfectionism also expands moral attention beyond avoiding harm: it asks whether we have reasons to develop our abilities and pursue worthwhile activities. At the same time, the criticisms remind us that promoting a supposed good can become coercive, unfair, or insensitive to reasonable differences among people.

important_terms.definition: The view that some things are valuable in themselves, rather than valuable only because people want them or find them pleasant.
A way of thinking about a good life as one that succeeds in valuable activities, relationships, and achievements, not merely one that feels good.
A version of perfectionism that connects valuable human activities with developing important features of human nature.
A version that lists or identifies valuable goods, such as knowledge or friendship, without grounding them in human nature.
The idea that different lives can be good in different ways, and that some goods may be equally valuable or impossible to rank.
A moral view that asks people to care about developing their own lives and, in some versions, helping others develop good lives too.
The idea that government should not choose among competing ideas of the good life, especially when citizens reasonably disagree.
The claim that government coercion is generally justified only to stop people from directly harming others.

questions_to_think_about: Is a life better when it includes achievement and understanding, even if it includes less pleasure?
Can people have different excellent lives because they have different talents and interests?
Should public money support activities that some citizens consider valuable but others do not?
Can a government encourage good choices without treating citizens like children?
Does allowing many valuable lifestyles solve the problem of government disagreement?
